transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Sofia with Redwood Inference, i'm the account lead for Avalon. quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya Rao: Maya here, Head of Infrastructure at Avalon.
[00:10] Liam Patel: Liam, security engineer.
[00:12] Grace Kim: Grace, platform product manager.
[00:15] Ethan Cho: Ethan from Redwood, solutions engineer.
[00:18] Sofia Martinez: Great. goal for today is to understand your requirements for a private deployment, network constraints, compliance bar, and what success looks like for a pilot. we'll cover high-level options and then next steps. sound good?
[00:30] Maya Rao: yep. main ask is we need isolation in our AWS org. we can't have data egress to public endpoints, and we need auditability and kms integration. low latency between our services and the inference endpoints is important, especially for fraud models.
[00:45] Sofia Martinez: understood. just to check, are you leaning private/vpc or dedicated reserved infra?
[00:52] Grace Kim: we'd prefer Private VPC first. dedicated is interesting but we need a private network connection and SSO/audit controls.
[00:58] Ethan Cho: ok good. quick overview: Redwood Private gives you a customer-dedicated control plane with private networking options. we support VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (private endpoints), and options for on-prem in some cases. typical pattern for customers with strict egress rules is PrivateLink endpoints into our service in the same AWS region, or VPC peering when you want direct routing.
[01:18] Liam Patel: can you clarify traffic flow with private link? like does traffic traverse internal aws backbone only?
[01:25] Ethan Cho: yes, with PrivateLink traffic stays on the aws network, it's not exposed to the public internet. we create an interface endpoint in your VPC that resolves to our NLB in our VPC or account; depending on your security policy we can set it up such that only specific subnets/security groups can talk to it.
[01:40] Maya Rao: what about peering? we have multiple accounts, we prefer peering if latency is lower.
[01:47] Ethan Cho: VPC peering gives you direct routing between your VPC and ours, lower hops, slightly lower latency. the tradeoff is peering requires route table updates and you have to manage cross-account peering if you have multiple accounts; for multi-account we sometimes recommend a Transit Gateway. both are supported.
[02:03] Grace Kim: do you support cross-region? our primary infra is us-east-1 but we also have DR in eu-west-1, data residency requirements might force something.
[02:12] Ethan Cho: we can deploy Private nodes in multiple regions. typically you choose the region that hosts most traffic for the pilot. if you have residency constraints, we can place models in eu-west-1, and traffic remains in region via PrivateLink or peering. note though that model artifacts and KV cache replication across regions increases cost and complexity.
[02:30] Liam Patel: on encryption — we want customer-managed keys, hsm-backed if possible. is that available?
[02:37] Ethan Cho: yes, we integrate with customer KMS for TLS keys and at-rest encryption. for HSM-backed keys we have an enterprise option; it's something we can scope for private deployments. we'll need to capture key rotation policy and whether you want our control plane storing any key metadata.
[02:52] Sofia Martinez: quick aside, we are SOC2 certified and have ISO docs; we'll send the package after this call.
[02:58] Grace Kim: thanks. also, how do you handle audit logs and request tracing? we need full request-level logs for compliance and debugging.
[03:06] Ethan Cho: we provide audit logs via your private s3 bucket or direct secure log delivery; we can stream to your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose. request tracing at token level is available in the console for debugging; for the pilot we can enable more verbose logs but filter PII.
[03:22] Maya Rao: latency numbers — can you share expected p99 latencies?
[03:26] Ethan Cho: ballpark depends on model size and instance type. for small-medium models on GPU-based private nodes in-region, 99th percentile for single-turn requests is often 150-400ms. for larger LLMs it can be higher. importantly, with peering or PrivateLink we avoid the public internet hop which reduces variance. we can run benchmarks with your sample traffic.
[03:46] Liam Patel: what about firewall rules and egress — do you require any outbound internet connectivity from our side?
[03:52] Ethan Cho: in PrivateLink and peering setups, we generally don't need your instances to make outbound connections to our public endpoints. there are control plane calls that may reach the management plane — for completely air-gapped deployments we'd look at on-prem package which has separate options. for cloud private deployments, we can minimize outbound dependencies and document required CIDRs and ports.
[04:12] Grace Kim: dr and failover — if our primary region goes down, can you failover to the other region seamlessly?
[04:18] Ethan Cho: we support failover but it's not fully automatic unless you configure multi-region nodes and a routing policy. fallback policies can be set so traffic routes to a compatible model variant in another region. that will impact latency since you'll cross regions. for pilot, we'd usually keep it single region and test failover manually.
[04:34] Maya Rao: what about ingress authentication — do you support mTLS?
[04:38] Ethan Cho: yes, we support mTLS for service-to-service authentication and we support token-based auth plus SSO for the console. for long-lived connections we can do client certs. we'll capture the flow you need in the deep dive.
[04:51] Sofia Martinez: can we talk about model version pinning and rollout? if we do a pilot with a particular model, what's the upgrade path?
[04:58] Ethan Cho: the control plane supports model version pinning per route. rollouts can be canary or percentage-based. for Private deployments, you get the same rollout APIs; we can also provide a read-only sandbox for testing new model versions before promoting.
[05:12] Grace Kim: latency vs cost — how do you recommend balancing? we want low latency for fraud but cost matters.
[05:19] Ethan Cho: common pattern is to run a smaller, quantized model as a hot path for latency-sensitive checks and fall back to a larger model for suspect cases, or use batching for throughput-y endpoints. we can size GPU types and batching policies to meet your SLOs. Redwood Optimize can suggest profiles based on your prompt set.
[05:37] Maya Rao: network ops question: we need to ensure provider doesn't add routes to our VPC that we don't authorize. is that standard?
[05:44] Ethan Cho: yes—we don't push arbitrary routes. peering requires you to accept the peering and update route tables on your side. PrivateLink uses interface endpoints you control. we'll document required permissions for creation.
[05:57] Liam Patel: SOC2 fine but do you support SAML SSO + SCIM for user provisioning?
[06:02] Sofia Martinez: yes, SAML + SCIM are supported for the console and RBAC. we'll include the SAML metadata example in the docs.
[06:10] Grace Kim: about pilot scope — we want to run fraud-inference traffic from our transaction API to Redwood for 3k requests/sec peak, average 600 qps. do you have throughput guidance?
[06:20] Ethan Cho: rough guidance: throughput depends on model cost per token and instance type. for 3k rps you may need a dedicated pool of GPUs or multiple replicas with autoscaling. for the pilot we usually provision enough Dedicated/Private capacity to simulate peak load and then tune batching and autoscale policies. we'll need a sample payload size and tokens/request to estimate.
[06:39] Maya Rao: we'll share sample payloads and token estimates.
[06:43] Ethan Cho: perfect. also, if you want to avoid any cross-account peering complexity, PrivateLink per region is usually faster to stand up for pilots. for multi-account setups, Transit Gateway is another option.
[06:56] Grace Kim: one more: can you restrict models available in our private deployment? some models need to be disallowed.
[07:02] Ethan Cho: yes, you can pin and restrict model catalog per tenant. we can curate allowed models and versions for compliance.
[07:10] Liam Patel: anything about data retention? we need data inferences not stored beyond X days and to control logs containing sensitive fields.
[07:16] Ethan Cho: we have retention policies by tenant; for private deployments we can configure shorter retention and we can redact or not log sensitive fields. we'll need to know retention window and exact PII policy.
[07:29] Sofia Martinez: ok going to recap and next steps— we'll send SOC2/ISO docs, network diagram templates, example PrivateLink and peering architectures, and an initial pilot pricing sheet. Ethan will schedule a deep-dive with your infra team to walk ports, CIDRs, and certs. Maya will share CIDRs and sample payloads. Liam will confirm KMS/HSM and retention policy.
[07:54] Maya Rao: sounds good. can we also get a timeline for a pilot? we're targeting january for a smoke test, then feb for a limited production window.
[08:03] Sofia Martinez: we can aim for that— we'll include timeline options in the pricing sheet.
[08:08] Grace Kim: any blockers from our side today?
[08:11] Liam Patel: just internal signoff on the pilot budget, but from security side the questions are clear.
[08:16] Ethan Cho: i'll put together the network diagrams and a checklist of required IAM perms and ports.
[08:21] Sofia Martinez: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email with artifacts.
[08:25] Maya Rao: thanks all.
[08:27] End of recording.
